extracted.intended_audience: peer reviewers for the International Journal of Machine Learning (IJML)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for conducting and writing peer reviews of manuscripts submitted to the International Journal of Machine Learning (IJML), including confidentiality, conflict checks, structuring reviews, major/minor issues to assess, recommendation categories, and scorecard attributes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competing Interests
rubrics_metrics.description: You should not accept a review assignment if you have a potential competing interest, including the following: Prior or current collaborations with the author(s); You are a direct competitor; You may have a known history of antipathy with the author(s); You might profit financially from the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Please inform the editors or journal staff and recuse yourself if you feel that you are unable to offer an impartial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality / Blind Review
rubrics_metrics.description: IJML performs blind reviews for manuscripts, so the identity of every reviewer is protected. Reviewers must treat the manuscripts as confidential documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manuscripts must not be shown to or discussed with others except with the authors’ permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept or Decline: suitability and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Before you accept or decline an invitation to review, consider: Does the article match your area of expertise? Do you have a potential conflict of interest? Do you have time?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the paper based on the title and abstract, only accept if you feel you can provide a high-quality review. Disclose conflicts to the editor when you respond. Accept or decline invitations quickly to prevent delays. If you decline, it is helpful to provide suggestions for alternative reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuring Your Review (four-part structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-part structure of moves is proposed for IJML review reports: Move 1: Summarizing judgment regarding suitability for publication; Move 2: Outlining the article; Move 3: Points of criticism (major issues and minor issues); Move 4: Conclusion and recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the four moves to make reviews clear and useful to editors and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review tone and presentation (tips)
rubrics_metrics.description: General tips on how to write the review: Give positive feedback first; Briefly summarize what the paper is about and what the findings are; Put the findings into context of existing literature; Indicate significance and novelty; Indicate strengths, quality, and completeness; State any major flaws or weaknesses; Note presentational problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are more likely to read your review if you give positive feedback first — but don't overdo it if you will be recommending rejection. Be courteous and constructive; do not include ad hominem remarks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Major Issues to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify any major flaws, their severity, and their impact on the paper’s validity or publishability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific considerations: Has a similar work already been published without acknowledgement? Are authors presenting findings that challenge current thinking and is evidence strong enough? Have they cited relevant contradictory work and addressed it? If major revisions are required, indicate clearly what they are. Are there major presentational problems (figures & tables, language, manuscript structure) that impede assessment? Are there any ethical issues (if unsure, disclose in confidential comments to editors)?

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor Issues to evaluate
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify smaller problems and corrections that do not undermine the main claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for ambiguous passages and suggest corrections; check references (missing, excessive, biased) and suggest additions; flag factual, numerical, or unit errors; ensure tables and figures are appropriate, sufficient, and correctly labelled.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation categories and reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: When you make a recommendation, consider the categories the editor will likely use: Reject; Accept without revision; Revise — either major or minor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain your reasoning in your report. If recommending revision, explain the revisions required and indicate whether you would be happy to review the revised article. Your recommendation is visible only to journal editors; there is the opportunity to direct separate comments to both the editor and author.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clear, supported judgments
rubrics_metrics.description: Your review should provide insight into any deficiencies and explain and support your judgment so that both editors and authors can fully understand the reasoning behind your comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support claims with evidence or examples from the manuscript; give constructive guidance on how to address deficiencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorecard / Rating: main research question relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the main question addressed by the research? Is it relevant and interesting?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to form your overall impression and to rate the manuscript on the importance and relevance of its central question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorecard / Rating: originality
rubrics_metrics.description: How original is the topic? What does it add to the subject area compared with other published material?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty and incremental contribution relative to existing literature; note whether the work is mainly confirmatory or offers new insight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorecard / Rating: writing quality and clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper well written? Is the text clear and easy to read?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider organization, clarity of exposition, and readability; flag language or structural issues that impede comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorecard / Rating: conclusions supported by evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the conclusions consistent with the evidence and arguments presented? Do they address the main question posed?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether results and analysis justify the claims made; point out overstatements or unsupported inferences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorecard / Rating: strength of contrarian claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If the author is disagreeing significantly with the current academic consensus, do they have a substantial case? If not, what would be required to make their case credible?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the thoroughness of evidence, consideration of counter-evidence, and engagement with the relevant literature when claims challenge consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorecard / Rating: figures and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: If the paper includes tables or figures, what do they add to the paper? Do they aid understanding or are they superfluous?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether visual elements are necessary, clear, correctly labelled, and whether they improve the reader's understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scorecard / Rating: English language appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the English language appropriate and understandable?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag grammatical issues, awkward phrasing, or language problems that hinder comprehension; indicate whether language revision is required for clarity.
